title: Kangana Ranaut Delivered a Baby While Terrorists Walked the Halls. This Is the 26/11 Story Nobody Told.
excerpt: Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata puts the nurses of Cama Hospital at the centre of India's darkest night — and the real woman behind it will make you ashamed you never knew her name.
body:
On the night of November 26, 2008, while terrorists stormed the Taj and the Oberoi and the nation watched in horror, a nurse named **Anjali Kulthe** was working the maternity ward at **Cama and Albless Hospital** in South Mumbai. Kasab and his partner had already entered the building. Gunfire echoed through the corridors. And Kulthe — unarmed, unprotected, utterly alone in her decision — gathered 20 pregnant women and walked them, in silence, to a locked room on another floor.

<youtube></youtube>

One of those women was high-risk. She went into labour during the siege. Kulthe delivered the baby the next morning, while the hospital was still under lockdown.

This is the story that **Kangana Ranaut**'s new film **Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata** wants you to know. And honestly, it should make you uncomfortable that you're only hearing it now.

The film — originally titled *Nurses of Cama* — is written and directed by **Manoj Tapadia**, and it does something genuinely rare in Indian cinema's 26/11 filmography: it ignores the terrorists almost entirely. No NSG commandos rappelling from helicopters. No Taj burning in slow motion. Instead, the camera stays inside the hospital, inside the wards, inside the fear. The heroes here aren't armed. They wear scrubs. They carry IV drips. And they made choices that night that saved over 400 lives.

Kangana plays a nurse modelled on Kulthe, and from the trailer, she's brought the right energy — controlled, fierce, stripped of the larger-than-life persona she sometimes leans into. This isn't *Manikarnika* on a horse. This is a woman in a dimly lit corridor trying to keep her voice steady while telling terrified patients to stay silent. It might be the most restrained thing Kangana has done in years, and that restraint looks like it could be devastating.

> "These are people we see every day, often without noticing them, yet their absence would bring the entire system to a halt." — Jayantilal Gada, producer

The ensemble cast is stacked with formidable Marathi and Hindi actresses — **Girija Oak**, **Smita Tambe**, **Amrutha Namdev**, **Esha Dey**, **Priya Berde**, **Asha Shelar**, and **Suhita Thatte** — each playing one of the hospital staff who held the line that night. Tapadia has reportedly drawn from testimonies of the actual nurses, and the real Anjali Kulthe later testified in court, confronting Kasab face-to-face. That detail alone is cinema.

The promotional campaign has been unconventional. Rather than the standard press junket, Kangana and Chhattisgarh Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai held a special screening in Raipur to honour real-life unsung heroes. The campaign has moved through Bhubaneswar, Jodhpur, and Delhi, honouring ordinary people who performed extraordinary acts of courage. It's the kind of grassroots outreach that feels more like a movement than a movie release — and that's exactly the energy Kangana has always been best at channelling when she decides the project is bigger than her.

For the diaspora, 26/11 occupies a unique wound. It was the attack that made home feel fragile. Many NRIs remember exactly where they were when the news broke — refreshing NDTV on office computers, calling family in Mumbai, watching the Taj burn on CNN with colleagues who had no idea what it meant. The stories of the commandos and the hostages have been told, retold, and dramatized. The story of a nurse delivering a baby while gunfire rattled the floor above her has not. That's the gap this film exists to fill. For NRIs, this film not only serves as a reminder of the vulnerability faced by loved ones back home but also highlights the resilience of those who work in the healthcare system, often risking their lives for others.

**Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata** is produced by **PEN Studios**, **Manikarnika Films**, and **Paramhans Creations**, and releases on **June 12** — the same Friday as **Main Vaapas Aaunga** and **Governor**. Three films, three defining moments in Indian history, one impossible weekend for Bollywood. This is the one that will make you cry.
